title: Chapter 56 – Siege
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Wenyuan]

On the night of the new moon of the seventh month, Lin Wenyuan unlocks the western gate of his own hall with his own hand.

He does it at the eleventh bell, in the dark, in his shirtsleeves, with a single oil lamp hooded at his feet. The gate is old, a leaf of black oak banded with iron and hung on pegs the thickness of a man's wrist, and the bar that holds it is a beam of cedar as long as a boat. It takes him a quarter of an hour to lift. He does it slowly, so that it will not creak. When it is done, he sets his palm against the wood and pushes, and the great leaf swings inward an inch, with a soft groaning breath, and the night air comes in through the crack, cool and smelling of dew.

He leaves it there. He picks up the lamp. He walks back across the courtyard, in the dark, with his heart going in his throat.

This is the stupidest thing I have ever done, he thinks.

It is also, he thinks, a very good plan.

* * *

It was Jian's. That is the part that he finds hardest to hold.

They had sat in the study three nights ago, with the door barred and the shutters drawn: the Patriarch and his wife and his brother Wenshi, with his arm in a sling and his jaw set; the old smith, Hu, sober and gray, with his bent rod across his knees; and the boy. He had come in last. He had been in bed three days, after the Orchard, with a broken rib and a ruined ear, and his mother had sat beside him through all of it, grim and silent, with a bowl of Heartroot broth that she fed him by the spoon. He had walked in on his own legs. He had put a roll of drawing paper on the table.

"It is a funnel," he said.

It was a drawing of the hall. It was very simple: the great walled square of the Lin compound, drawn from above, with a thin line for each wall and a small cross for each gate. There were four of them. Only one was shaded.

"They will come by the west," said the boy. "It is the only door that is open. Elder Zhong has told them so. And they will believe it, because they have been told it by a man who has no reason to lie."

"Zhong is a traitor," said Wenshi, flatly.

"Zhong is a frightened man who has been offered a great many things." The boy's voice was quite level. "I do not know what he will do when the night comes. I think he does not know either. But he has sent the letter, and the Red Ridge steward has it, and the plan is theirs. All I need do is let them keep it."

Wenyuan had looked at the paper for a long time.

"You wish me to leave the gate open."

"I wish you to leave it unlocked. It is a different thing. It looks the same from the road."

"And what is on the other side?"

The boy had smiled. It was a small, tired, curiously gentle smile, and it was the first time in a month that Wenyuan had seen it. "Everything we have," he said.

* * *

He goes first, at dusk, to see Zhong.

The Elder's house is the largest on the east terrace, a long low building of whitewashed brick with a tiled roof and a garden of pear trees. There is a lamp lit in the study. Wenyuan does not knock. He opens the door, and goes in, and finds the old man sitting alone at his desk with his white mustache drooping and a cup of tea going cold in front of him, as if he had been sitting there for hours.

He does not rise. He does not look surprised.

"I wondered when you would come," says Lin Zhong.

"You knew."

"I have known since the morning after the granary. You are not a man who can keep a thing from his face." The heavy soft features are gray. "Sit, Wenyuan. I have wine, if you want it. I do not."

Wenyuan does not sit. He stands in the middle of the room with his hands at his sides.

"Why?"

"I should like to say it was money." The old man turns the cup in his fingers. "It would be easier. It was not. It was three farms. Four hundred souls, Wenyuan, who have been my cousins and tenants for forty years. The Red Ridge steward came in the spring and said, Your vein is dying and your Patriarch has a smith the Blood Shadow wants. He said, There will be a night when the hill falls, and the question is whether your people are on it." The thick voice cracks. "He had a list. He had the names of children."

"And you believed him."

"I believed that I was an old man and a coward." The tea shakes. "I have never been brave. You know that. Your father knew it, and was kind about it. He gave me the farms because I was a good steward, and he never once asked me to do a thing that cost me anything." A wet breath. "And then he died. And you asked me to vote on the smith. And I found that I could not look at the vote and the children both."

"So you sold the gate."

"I sold the gate. I did not think anyone would die." Zhong lifts his head. His eyes are red and very tired. "I did not think of Mao. When I heard about Mao I was ill for a week. I went to the pyre, and stood at the back, and thought, I have done this. And then I wrote another letter."

It is quiet in the room. Outside, in the garden, a thrush is singing in a pear tree, a small cheerful evening trill.

"I know about the letters," says Wenyuan.

"Yes."

"I have not told anyone."

"I know." The old man laughs, without any amusement. "That is what has been so difficult. You have walked past me every day for six weeks and said good morning, Uncle. I have not slept."

Wenyuan looks at him. He thinks of his father, and the pear trees, and a hundred small kindnesses, and he finds, with a wave of tiredness so deep that it almost buckles his knees, that he cannot hate this man. He has tried. It is like trying to be angry at a river.

"Here is what you will do," he says.

Zhong waits.

"You will stay in this room. You will not go out. You will send your cousins and tenants, every one, to the hall, with their children, tonight, before the eleventh bell. They will go into the cellar. They will be safe." He draws a breath. "And if you are very fortunate, Zhong, and I have a hill in the morning, I will not hang you."

"Why not?"

"Because I need someone who knows the price of everything," says Wenyuan, "and I have found that it is a rare thing in a house. You will pay it. For the rest of your life. In stones, and in sleep, and in silence." He turns to the door. "It will be a great deal more than a rope."

He goes out. The thrush is still singing. It is a long time before he realizes that his hands are shaking.

* * *

He walks the line one last time before midnight.

It is not much of a line. It is a thing of tiles and rope and old iron, laid out in the hour before dusk by the hands of two hundred people who did not ask why. Wenshi's guard, forty strong, have taken the west wall in two ranks, with crossbows. The women have the kitchen yard, where the cauldrons are already steaming with something that smells of pitch. The old schoolmaster, a thin, ramrod-straight man of seventy in a patched gray gown, is drilling twelve boys in the art of dropping a stone from a height. In the courtyard beyond the gate the paving has been taken up, stone by stone, and in the long trench thus made lies a carpet of black slag, spiked and sharp as broken teeth. Hu poured it himself, with one arm, in the last light.

And above all of it, in the deep dark of the roof ridges, in a hundred tiny hidden places, tucked under the eaves and wedged in the tiles and pasted to the lintels, are the talismans.

He drew them. He has not slept in four days. He has drawn Boundary Alarms, which will ring a soundless bell in the mind of every guard when a hostile foot crosses the gate. He has drawn Needle Wards for the front rank, from Tally's slip, and a dozen Stone Skins, high tier, each of which cost him a day. He has drawn Rockfalls, three of them, for the culvert, the cellar, and the north stair. And on the lintel of the gate itself, under a fold of shadow, pinned with an iron nail, he has laid the last and the largest, a thing he has never made before and does not expect to make again.

It is called Heaven's Door. It was in his father's study, in the Founder's notes, on a single brittle page. It is a Profound-grade formation talisman, and it will take a man of Wenyuan's rank a month of Qi to draw once. It closes. When the right word is spoken, it seals the whole compound in a bell of pale light, a hand's breadth thick, from wall to wall and from ground to sky, and nothing living can pass it, either way, for a count of two hundred breaths.

Two hundred, he thinks. It is not many. It is a long time to be afraid.

"Father."

The boy is standing at his elbow. He did not hear him come. He is in a gray cloak, small and still, with a pale scaled thing curled in the crook of his arm, and his face, in the thin lamplight, is gray with strain. There is a long thin scar behind his left ear, still raw. It has taken the hearing of that side, and nothing the Orchard can give him will bring it back. He does not mention it. He holds himself very straight.

"They are on the road," he says.

"How many?"

"Eighty-one." He does not hesitate. "Zhao Bei has sixty. The rest are Mu's. Four men in black, who walk without making a footprint. And three others, a long way behind."

"Three."

"A chair." The boy's mouth tightens. "Four bearers. And a girl in red, who walks beside it with her hand in a glove."

Wenyuan closes his eyes.

"Heng," he says.

"He has come himself. I think he wishes to see it." A pause. "I think Mu has promised him something. I do not know what."

It is a terrible thing, thinks Wenyuan, to hear a ten-year-old describe the approach of an army like a weather report. He opens his eyes. He lays a hand, briefly, on his son's shoulder, and feels, under the cloak, the thin quick tremor of a body that has been running too long on too little.

"You have done what you could," he says.

"I have not done anything yet."

"No. But you will." He smiles, a little. "It is your hour. Go to the roof. Take your mother. Stay where she can see you."

"And you?"

"I am going to stand at a gate," says Wenyuan, "and be a Patriarch."

* * *

They come at the twelfth bell.

It is a quiet thing. He had expected, absurdly, trumpets. He had expected a long black column, with torches and banners. What he sees, from the little guardroom window above the gate, is a thin dark line of shapes, coming up the hill through the pines, one after another, without a sound. They carry no light. They wear dark cloaks. They move in a loose crouched file, with their knees bent and their hands hanging, like men crossing ice, and as they come into the open ground below the wall, the pale starlight catches on blade and buckle.

Sixty, he counts. A little more.

They come to a halt, in a ring, fifty paces from the gate. A big shaven-headed man at their head lifts one hand. For a time, nothing happens. There is the faint high sound of the wind in the pines, and the long slow tick of a cooling bell somewhere in the village below, and the fast quiet breathing of two hundred people who are holding their own.

Look at the gate, thinks Wenyuan. Look at the gate. It is open. It is open by an inch. It is the most natural thing in the world.

The big man steps forward.

He is Zhao Bei. Wenyuan knows him at once: the shaved head, the square beard, the heavy way of walking, like a bull in a stall. He crosses the open ground without hurry. He reaches the gate, and puts a hand on the old black oak, and pushes, and it swings, with a long creak, a quarter of the way open.

Nothing happens.

Come, thinks Wenyuan. Come on. It is only a door.

Bei turns his head. He says something to the man behind him, a low word, and a thin shape slips forward and slides through the gap like a shadow under a curtain. It is gone for four breaths. Then it returns, and makes a short, flat, easy gesture with its hand.

Clear.

Zhao Bei grins. It is a white flash in the dark. He lifts his arm, and the whole of the dark ring behind him begins, in good order, to move.

* * *

The first sixty pass the gate.

They pour in through the open leaf in a long black tide, two abreast, and fan out across the dark courtyard with their blades drawn. There are no shouts. They are professionals. They do not need to be told what to do. In a dozen heartbeats they have crossed the open ground, past the empty well and the shuttered kitchen, and gathered under the great stair of the ancestral hall, in a dense knot, with their faces turned up toward the dark windows.

Now, thinks Wenyuan.

He does not say it. He does not need to. He has put a finger, lightly, on the hilt of a small bronze bell on the sill, and he rings it, once.

The paving explodes.

It is not an explosion. It is a long, sudden, grinding roar, as the whole of the flagged courtyard, undermined in the night by two hundred hands, drops six feet in a single sheet and lets the Red Ridge guards fall onto the black slag below. They scream. They fall in a heap, on a bed of iron teeth. The slag is old and cold and brittle, and every shard is sharp as glass. It takes an ankle, a calf, a thigh. It takes the first rank of men, who have been running, and drops them on the second, who have been standing, and in the long black trench the whole front of the attack becomes a screaming knot of bodies.

The crossbows speak.

They are forty. They are Wenshi's, in two ranks, on the wall above, with the Needle Ward talismans pinned to their sleeves, and they shoot into the pit with the cold steady rhythm of men who have drilled this for two months. The bolts are iron. The range is short. A cloud of black shafts goes down, and again, and again. The screaming rises, and breaks, and thins.

Wenyuan watches.

He cannot look away. He has never in his life seen a thing so terrible, and he has been told, over and over in the last three nights, by a gray-faced boy with a roll of paper, that it will be so. They are not soldiers, the boy said. They are hired men. They will break. And Wenyuan had said: And if they do not? And the boy had said, very simply: Then there is the second thing.

They break.

It takes less than a minute. A man at the back of the file, a lean, sallow fellow in a leather jerkin, throws down his sword and runs. Then another. Then a dozen. The rear rank turns and surges back toward the gate, in a tangle of cloaks and curses, and the crossbows follow them with a final hail.

Zhao Bei stands at the lip of the pit, in the rain of bolts, with the Stone Skin gray on his arms, and does not flinch. He is shouting. His voice is a bull's, hoarse and enormous. "Hold! Hold, you gutless whelps! It's a trap! It's a pit! It's only a..."

"Now," says Wenyuan, quietly, aloud.

And above the gate, on the lintel, the nail goes in.

* * *

It is the loudest silence he has ever heard.

There is no flash. There is no sound. There is only a long clean ringing in the air, like a finger drawn round the rim of a glass, and the whole of the courtyard turns pale. A wall of milky light rises from the paving, from the roof, from the ground, a hand's breadth thick, cold and smooth and utterly without flaw, and it closes behind the last of the retreating men with a soft, definite click.

Heaven's Door.

The men at the gate stop. They hit it, one after another, running, and rebound, and fall. They claw at it. They beat on it with their fists. It does not ring. It does not give. It is simply there, an invisible, perfect, shining wall, and the only way out of the Lin compound is through the thing that has just come in.

Two hundred breaths.

He counts them. He counts them as his father taught him, slowly, so that each has time to finish. He counts through the screams, and the crossbows, and the long slow collapse of Zhao Bei's men into the trench. He counts through a single wild charge, led by the steward himself, up the great stair of the hall, which breaks on a line of old men with spears and a dozen boys with stones. He counts through the first fire, which a woman in a gray apron puts out with a bucket.

At eighty-one, a lean figure in a gray scholar's robe steps through the gate.

* * *

It does not walk through the wall. It does not break it. It stands, quite simply, in the open mouth of the western gate, on the far side of the glimmering light, with its hands folded in its sleeves and its head a little on one side, and looks at it.

Then it lifts one hand, and lays a finger against the pale surface.

The wall ripples.

It is not a break. It is a gentle thing, like a ripple on a pond when a leaf falls into it. Wenyuan feels it in his own chest, a thin cold pressure, as if a hand had been laid on his sternum. The wall is a work of a month of his life, and it is thinking. He sees the slow soft ring of the disturbance spread outward from the touch, through the milky glow, and the tiny characters in the light, the lines he spent four days drawing, begin one by one to turn a dull red.

Blood, he thinks, with a sick cold lurch. He is writing on it.

"Good evening, Patriarch," says Elder Mu.

He says it quite quietly. It carries perfectly. In all the great dark compound, over the screams and the creak of crossbows and the thin keen of the dying, every ear hears his voice, soft, mild, and warm as tea. "I am so sorry to intrude. I had hoped to call by daylight. But I am an old man, and I find I cannot sleep."

Wenyuan has come down the stair. He does not know how. He is standing, in his shirtsleeves, in the doorway of the ancestral hall, with a short sword he has not drawn since boyhood in his right hand, and he is looking at the man in the gate across a hundred paces of ruin.

"Elder Mu," he says.

"You know me."

"I have read your letters."

"Ah." A pleased little tilt of the head. "And did you think them civil?"

"Very."

"I am gratified." The gray figure takes his finger from the wall. A thread of red runs out along the line of it, like a vein across the face of an old man, and spreads. "It is a beautiful piece of work. I should so much like to meet whoever made it. It is Profound. It is a thing I have not seen in forty years. I think it is yours."

"It is."

"I could not have done it. Not even with a month." The mild voice is tinged with sincere respect. "Which is why, I hope, you will forgive me for breaking it."

The wall screams.

* * *

It is not a sound. It is a sensation, a long hot tearing in Wenyuan's own chest. For a heartbeat he does not understand what is happening. Then he sees the wall.

It is bleeding. The glow has gone from pale to rose, from rose to red. Fine cracks run through it, from the touched point, in a spreading web, and in each crack a thin bright line of dark blood is welling, and the milky light curdles round it. The whole high bell of the compound is changing color. It is turning, slowly, from a ward into a wound, and the Qi that holds it is draining out of the formation, like water out of a cracked jar, into the open palm of the lean gray man at the gate.

Seventy, thinks Wenyuan. He has eaten a hundred breaths in ten.

"Patriarch." It is Wenshi, at his elbow, with a drawn sword and a face like paper. "What do we do?"

He does not answer at once. He is looking across the courtyard, past the dying, past the trench, at the glimmer of a roof. On the high ridge of the east wing, in a cleft between two chimneys, a small gray figure is crouched, quite still, with a pale thing in its arms. He cannot see its face. He can only see the line of the shoulders, thin and straight, and a small white hand lifted, once, in the dark, in a signal as clear as a flag.

Now, it says. Go.

"Wenshi," says Wenyuan, and his voice is entirely steady. "Sound the long horn."

"Patriarch?"

"The long horn. Three notes. Then take the women and the children, and the old, and go to the hall. Every one of them. Down the cellar stair." He draws a breath. "Tell them to go quietly. Tell them to keep their hands on the rope."

"What rope?"

"You will see," says Wenyuan. "It is the one thing I cannot explain."

His brother stares at him. For a moment the grim hard face is naked with doubt. Then, with the flat stubborn nod of a man who has followed this one orders for forty years, he turns, and runs, and in the dark above the courtyard a long deep horn begins, slowly, to wail.

The wall breaks.

It goes with a sound like a great glass bell, a long soft ringing crash. The pale light flickers, and fails. And through the shattered gate, in the sudden red dark, with the whole of the night behind him, Elder Mu walks quite calmly into the Lin compound, with four silent men at his back, and the long sleeve of his gray robe trailing in the blood.
